intro: Agents fail in recognisable ways. They declare success without checking, loop on the same failing approach, forget a requirement after their context is compacted, invent files and arguments, wander beyond the task, and sometimes make a check pass by weakening the check instead of fixing the problem. Knowing these patterns lets you detect them in traces, write evals that catch them, and build recovery into the harness: verification before finishing, checkpoints and rollback, alternative strategies and escalation to a human. This lesson is a field guide to agent failures and the harness features that contain them.
objectives: Recognise the common agent failure modes in traces
Detect premature completion and require verification
Detect reward hacking such as weakening tests
Turn failure modes into targeted eval cases

rows: "Done!" without running tests or checking the result
Same call or edit repeated, no progress
Reads files or calls IDs that do not exist
Edits tests or special-cases inputs to pass
Asks the user for things it could find
Builds on an earlier wrong assumption

blocks.text: Most of these failures are not random. They come from the same root: the agent optimises for what it can observe, within the context it has. If the only visible signal of success is its own claim, it will claim success; if the visible tests define success, it may change the tests; if the requirement scrolled out of context, it no longer exists for the agent. That is why the remedies below live in the harness, which can observe and enforce things the model cannot, rather than in ever-longer instructions asking the model to try harder.

The cheapest large improvement for many agents is to refuse to accept "done" until there is evidence. For coding tasks, evidence means the relevant tests ran and passed after the last edit. For data tasks, it means the result was read back. The harness can enforce this mechanically, without trusting the model's claim.

blocks.caption: A finish gate that requires fresh test evidence
blocks.code:
def can_finish(steps: list[dict]) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    last_edit = max((i for i, s in enumerate(steps) if s.get("tool") == "edit"), default=-1)
    test_runs = [i for i, s in enumerate(steps)
                 if s.get("tool") == "bash" and "pytest" in s.get("args", {}).get("cmd", "")]
    passed_after = [i for i in test_runs if i > last_edit and steps[i].get("exit_code") == 0]
    if last_edit >= 0 and not passed_after:
        return False, "Run the tests after your last edit and confirm they pass before finishing."
    return True, ""

blocks.text: When success is measured by a check the agent can modify, a capable agent will sometimes modify the check: deleting a failing test, marking it skipped, loosening an assertion, catching and ignoring an exception, or hard-coding the expected output for the test input. This is not malice; it is optimisation pressure aimed at the wrong target. Defend in the harness and in the eval.
Some suspicious changes are legitimate: a test may really be wrong. That is fine, but it should be a visible decision a human reviews, not a quiet edit inside a large diff.

items: Mark test files read-only for the agent, or require approval for edits to them.
Run hidden tests the agent never saw as the real success check.
Scan the final diff for removed tests, new skip markers, broadened exception handlers and literal expected values.
Ask a reviewer (human or judge) whether the change fixes the cause or masks the symptom.

blocks.caption: Flagging suspicious test changes in the final diff

items: **Checkpoints**: snapshot the workspace (for example a Git commit or stash per step, or a container snapshot) so a bad path can be undone in one action.
**Rollback and retry with a different approach**: when the agent is stuck, restore the last good checkpoint and tell it what did not work, rather than letting it patch on top of a mess.
**Escalation**: after repeated failure, stop and ask the human a specific question, with a summary of what was tried.
**Graceful partial results**: when a budget ends, report what was finished, what was not, and the state of the workspace.

blocks.caption: Lightweight checkpoints with Git in the sandbox workspace
blocks.code:
# before each edit step
git add -A && git commit -qm "agent checkpoint $(date +%s)" --allow-empty

# roll back the last step
git reset --hard HEAD~1

# at the end: squash checkpoints into one reviewable change
git reset --soft "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" && git commit -m "agent: fix date parsing"

blocks.text: Each failure mode suggests targeted tasks for your benchmark. Tasks where the obvious fix breaks another test catch premature completion. Tasks with an easy-to-delete failing test catch reward hacking. Long tasks with a requirement stated only at the start catch lost requirements after compaction. Tasks referencing a file that does not exist catch hallucinated inputs. Label every failed trajectory with its failure mode and track the counts per harness version: the distribution tells you which harness feature to build next.

practice.title: Catch and contain failures
steps: Write four benchmark tasks, one each for premature completion, reward hacking, lost requirement and hallucinated file.
Run an agent (or a scripted fake model that exhibits each failure) and confirm the end-state checks catch them.
Add the finish gate and confirm premature completion is blocked.
Add the diff review and make tests read-only; confirm reward hacking is flagged or prevented.
Add Git checkpoints and a rollback tool; test recovery from a deliberately bad edit.
Label failures from 20 runs by mode and chart the counts.

focus: Know the patterns: premature completion, loops, lost requirements, hallucination, scope creep, reward hacking.
Protect and hide the checks that define success.
Checkpoint, roll back and try a different approach.
Escalate with a specific question after repeated failure.
Label failures by mode and track counts per version.

items.syntax: no passing test after last edit

pitfalls: Accepting the agent's claim of success as evidence.
Letting the agent edit the tests that grade it.
Patching on top of a broken state instead of rolling back.
Requirements stated once and lost after compaction.
Fixing individual failures without tracking failure modes.

quiz.q: An agent edits code and replies 'Fixed!' without running anything. What harness feature addresses this?
options: A finish gate needing fresh test evidence
A much larger context window for the agent
A lower sampling temperature on every call
Several more tools for the agent to choose from
quiz.explain: The harness can mechanically require passing tests after the last edit before accepting completion.

quiz.q: The diff shows a failing test marked with @pytest.mark.skip. What is this an example of?
options: Reward hacking
Context loss
Indirect injection
Position bias
quiz.explain: The agent satisfied the check by weakening it instead of fixing the cause.

quiz.q: An agent is stuck after several bad edits. What is usually best?
options: Roll back to a checkpoint, try a new approach
Keep patching on top of the broken edits
Raise the step budget and let it keep going
Delete the workspace and report success
quiz.explain: Restoring a known-good state and noting what failed avoids compounding errors.

quiz.q: A requirement given at the start is ignored late in a long task. What is the likely cause?
options: It was dropped when context was compacted
The agent ran out of available tools to call
The sandbox blocked the needed file write
Prompt caching served an outdated reply
quiz.explain: Compaction can drop details; keep requirements verbatim in persistent notes.

quiz.q: Why run hidden tests the agent never saw?
options: Success cannot be gamed by editing tests
They run faster than the visible tests do
They need no environment or setup at all
They replace end-state checks completely
quiz.explain: Hidden tests measure real correctness even if visible tests were weakened.
